title: A Quiet Failure in Calibrated Virtual Screening: Marginal Conformal Prediction Under-Covers the Minority Class, and a Class-Conditional Fix Recovers It
abstract: Conformal prediction is being adopted in drug discovery to put an honest number on model reliability: pick an error rate alpha, and the method returns prediction sets containing the true label with probability at least 1 - alpha. We show this guarantee can be dangerous on imbalanced datasets. Across four datasets, standard (marginal) conformal prediction hits its global 90% coverage target while leaving the minority class badly exposed: realized minority coverage falls to 64.8% on blood-brain-barrier penetration and to 4.2% on clinical-trial toxicity, where the rare class is nearly abandoned. The failure is not tied to one model: a random forest, a graph network, and a frozen chemical language model all reproduce it (p < 0.001 in every case), with severity tracking baseline calibration on rare labels rather than architecture. A conservation identity explains the effect: the minority's shortfall equals the majority's surplus amplified by the imbalance ratio, predicting the measured gap to within one point and ordering severity across datasets. The failure survives realistic scaffold splits and a second conformal score, while aggregate accuracy and overall coverage stay reassuringly high, which is exactly why it is easy to miss. Class-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction closes the gap on every dataset, restoring minority coverage to target for a modest increase in prediction-set size. We localize the failures to generic molecular scaffolds - plain benzene and pyridine cores occurring in both classes - propose a one-number diagnostic, and show with a cost model that abstaining on affected compounds flips a screening campaign from net-negative to net-positive utility. Our contribution is demonstrating on real chemistry how severe and invisible this known conformal-theory gap becomes under imbalance, and laying out a practical protocol restoring per-class reliability.

title: OrchardBench: A Physically-Grounded, GPU-Parallel Apple-Orchard Simulation Benchmark for Agricultural Robotics
abstract: Robotic tree-fruit harvesting is a flagship problem for agricultural automation, but progress is bottlenecked by the cost and irreproducibility of field experiments: an orchard is available only weeks a year, every tree is different, and a control error can permanently damage the crop or the plant. The tree models used in graphics and agronomy are geometrically detailed but physically inert, while the GPU-parallel simulators used in robot learning contain no plausible trees. We present OrchardBench, a physically-grounded, GPU-parallel simulation of apple-orchard trees on the Newton engine. Each tree is grown by a stochastic L-system and instantiated as a fully articulated body: branches are compliant torsional spring-dampers whose stiffness follows Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, they break at a wood modulus of rupture and fall as free hinges, and apples are independent bodies on stem tethers that detach at literature-grounded pull forces and load the branch when pulled. A moving, density-controllable foliage layer occludes the canopy as real leaves do. Every physical parameter is tied to a published source. Per-environment domain randomization makes each batched world a distinct tree, and a mobile manipulator with a wrist depth camera closes the loop with geometric fruit perception and an autonomous harvesting baseline. Careful engineering of the solver and the model lets OrchardBench run many parallel environments at interactive rates on a laptop GPU. We define the tasks and a metric suite spanning harvest completeness, throughput, and plant damage (with a per-canopy-zone breakdown), and report baseline results across foliage, fruit load, terrain, canopy zone, and parallelism. The analytic baseline succeeds on about 40% of the fruit it detects and harvests only about an eighth of the reachable fruit on a tree, leaving clear headroom for novel autonomy approaches.

title: Reward-Density Heuristic for Dynamic Multi-Vehicle Routing: Performance and Computational Efficiency
abstract: The Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) and its variants represent some of the most practically consequential optimization challenges in modern logistics and urban mobility. In this study, we address a dynamic, online variant combining elements of the VRP and the Orienteering Problem (OP), in which a fleet of vehicles must maximise cumulative reward collected within a fixed time horizon while continuously replanning as new tasks arrive. We propose and evaluate a reward-density heuristic for dynamic multi-vehicle assignment, referred to as the Efficiency heuristic. We evaluate this formulation across two application domains: autonomous drone task allocation and urban taxi dispatch, across multiple fleet sizes and task scales. The proposed method is compared with four classical construction heuristics and three metaheuristic algorithms (Adaptive Large Neighbourhood Search, Genetic Algorithm, and Simulated Annealing), all evaluated under identical conditions. Across all tested configurations, the Efficiency heuristic matches the solution quality of the best metaheuristic algorithms while requiring two to three orders of magnitude less planning time, establishing Pareto dominance over all competing methods on the reward-versus-compute frontier. These findings suggest a practical design principle for real-time allocation and dispatch systems: in dynamic, time-constrained routing environments, carefully designed greedy heuristics can match the output of sophisticated search procedures at a fraction of the computational cost, making them preferable for online deployment.

title: Evaluating Agentic Reasoning Patterns for Financial Data Analytics: A Domain-Specific Benchmark for ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, and Reflexion
abstract: The deployment of AI agents into production financial data systems has accelerated faster than the supporting evaluation infrastructure. Engineering teams selecting between reasoning patterns — ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, Reflexion, and their variants — rely on general-purpose benchmarks (HumanEval, MMLU, AgentBench) that measure capabilities only loosely correlated with production performance on financial analytics tasks. The result is a measurement gap: pattern preferences derived from general benchmarks may not predict pattern performance on the specific class of tasks that production financial agents actually execute. This paper presents Jasus-Bench, an open-source benchmark designed specifically to evaluate agentic reasoning patterns on financial data analytics tasks. The benchmark contains twenty representative tasks across four complexity classes (simple lookups, multi-table aggregations, time-series analysis, and anomaly detection), with deterministic test data generated through reproducible scripts and ground truth answers computed programmatically from the generated data. We describe the benchmark design, the experimental methodology, and the projected results that the methodology is expected to produce when full empirical evaluation completes. Publication versioning note. This paper is released as Version 1.0 covering the framework architecture, benchmark design, experimental methodology, and projected results derived from structural analysis and limited validation runs. Full empirical evaluation against three reasoning patterns across multiple LLM providers (estimated nine hundred experimental runs) is in active progress at time of publication. A Version 2.0 release will follow within approximately twelve weeks, replacing the projected results in Section 5 with measured empirical findings while preserving the methodology, benchmark design, and architectural contributions documented here. The v1 release establishes the framework and methodology for community evaluation and extension; the v2 release will provide the measured empirical foundation for production pattern selection decisions. The benchmark is the first of its kind for financial data analytics specifically. Existing benchmarks either measure general capabilities (HumanEval for coding, MMLU for knowledge) or measure tabular reasoning without financial domain context (Spider, BIRD, FinQA). Jasus-Bench addresses the specific intersection of agentic reasoning, structured data manipulation, and financial domain semantics where production agent deployments actually operate. The framework is released under MIT license at https://github.com/suhasgr09/jasus-bench, with reproducible data generation, hash-verified test artifacts, and mock-mode operation for cost-free CI integration. We argue that the AI agent ecosystem requires domain-specific evaluation infrastructure analogous to the way software ecosystems developed domain-specific testing frameworks: general benchmarks measure general capabilities, but production decisions require production-relevant measurement. The contribution of this paper is both the benchmark itself and the methodological argument that domain-specific evaluation is a necessary complement to general benchmarking, not an optional refinement of it.

title: Two Regimes of Failure in Structural Repair
abstract: We present a deterministic, oracle-verified engine for studying when the structural repair of a typed system fails. A structural system is a typed graph whose edges may violate jurisdiction rules between planes; a repair mechanism attempts to descend an integer interference functional to a normal form. The primary contribution is methodological: an engine whose behavior is validated against a frozen reference (dual continuous integration), with an explicit artifact control —a step-budget flag— that separates genuine failure from measurement noise. Using it, we characterize failure in two regimes. In the first (repair by deletion, forbidden on protected edges), failure occurs on a frontier in the contamination–irreparability plane with closed form, (1−T·p) to the power of the number of violating edges; this regime corresponds to terminating rewriting and serves as a control. In the second (repair by relocation, deletion forbidden), the system can settle into a structural local minimum: a stable configuration that is not the normal form. Across 62 parameter cells at R=500 replications, with zero artifact flags, the frequency of this trap increases monotonically with system size and plane count (saturating) and decreases with per-node entanglement; an apparent interior peak observed at low replication is shown to be sampling noise. This second regime is consistent with the satisfiability phase transition known in constraint-satisfaction problems (CSP), and admits an interpretation as a structural analogue of cusp bistability. The value of the work is the measured contrast between a trivial and an emergent failure mode, established with an audited instrument, and the operational integration of three separate formalisms —rewriting, catastrophe, and CSP— into a single executable system.

title: Interface-Binding Failures in Verifiable Privacy-Preserving Data Aggregation (3PDA cryptanalysis and repair)
abstract: Reproducible artifact for the cryptanalysis of 3PDA (Liu et al., IEEE TII 2019). Includes faithful proof-of-concept attacks with two independent real Type-1 symmetric-pairing backends (a self-contained pure-Python reduced Tate pairing and the Stanford PBC library), the C2 repair proof-obligation checks with a member-set-only negative ablation, 18 invariant tests, a frozen result snapshot with manifest hashes, and the LaTeX table generator. Deterministic results are byte-reproducible for fixed code/dependencies; timing rows are machine-dependent.
